commitResults.messageBody:
The chatbot only displays its banner, which does not acknowledge the
user or indicate that the session has ended.

Add a greeting and farewell between horizontal separators so the
initial program provides a complete, clearly delimited interaction
before exiting.

commitResults.messageTitle: Bott.java: Echo user input and exit on bye
commitResults.messageBody:
Bott currently only prints a greeting and a fixed farewell message;
it does not read or respond to anything the user types.

A chatbot needs to acknowledge user input and provide a way for the
user to end the session.

Let's read input line by line and echo each line back inside the
existing divider-block format, looping until the user types "bye",
at which point the farewell message is printed and the program
exits. Extract the shared 4-space divider indent into an INDENT
constant so the divider and the message text it wraps can never
drift out of alignment.

Echoing the raw input rather than parsing it keeps this step simple
while still exercising the message-formatting convention already in
place; command parsing can build on top of this once introduced.

commitResults.messageTitle: Bott.java: Add ability to store and list tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
Bott can only echo the user's input back; it has no way to keep
track of anything the user has told it, and "list" is not yet a
recognized command.

Users need a way to record short pieces of text (tasks) during a
session and see them again later, without requiring persistence to
disk at this stage.

Let's store each entered line in a fixed-size String[100] array
(per the task requirement's assumption of at most 100 tasks) and
acknowledge it with "added: <text>". Add a "list" command that
prints the stored tasks as a numbered list, built by a small
formatTaskList() helper so that numbering/formatting logic stays
separate from printMessage()'s job of wrapping text in dividers.

A fixed-size array keeps the implementation simple for now; a
resizable collection (e.g. ArrayList) can replace it later if the
100-task assumption is lifted.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add Task class and mark/unmark commands
commitResults.messageBody:
Bott currently stores each entered line as a plain String; there is
no way to record whether a task has been completed, and "mark" and
"unmark" are not recognized as commands.

Users need to track which tasks are done, and toggle that status
back and forth, per the task extension.

Let's introduce a Task class that pairs a description with an
isDone flag and knows how to render itself as "[X] desc" or
"[ ] desc". Bott's task array becomes Task[] instead of String[],
"list" now prints a header line followed by each task's numbered
status line, and "mark N"/"unmark N" locate the Nth task, flip its
status via markAsDone()/markAsNotDone(), and print the confirmation
message.

Using a class instead of a second parallel array (e.g. a matching
boolean[] for done-status) keeps a task's description and status
together as one unit and matches the A-Classes extension's guidance
to model a task as an object rather than primitive fields spread
across arrays.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add Todo, Deadline, and Event task types
commitResults.messageBody:
Bott can only create untyped Task objects from a bare line of text;
it has no way to represent a task's due date or start/end times, and
there is no command to distinguish the three kinds of tasks the
requirement calls for.

Let's add Todo, Deadline, and Event, each extending Task and
overriding toString() to prepend its type icon ("[T]"/"[D]"/"[E]")
and append any date/time fields, per the A-Inheritance extension.
Replace the old freeform-text add path in Bott with "todo", "deadline
... /by ...", and "event ... /from ... /to ..." commands, each
building the matching subclass and going through a shared addTask()
helper that stores the task and prints the "Got it... Now you have N
tasks" confirmation.

Storing all three subclasses in a single Task[] (rather than a
separate array per type) relies on polymorphism to keep list/mark/
unmark working unchanged, as the extension recommends. Dates/times
are kept as plain strings with no parsing, since converting them to
real date/time values isn't required yet.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add test-ui skill and console UI test plan
commitResults.messageBody:
Bott's behavior can only be checked by manually typing commands into
the running program and eyeballing the output; there's no recorded
set of test cases, and the previous automated approach (the
text-ui-test shell scripts) was removed as too primitive to be worth
maintaining.

Let's add test/ui-test-plan.md, recording ordered test cases — each
with an aim, the exact input lines to send, and the exact expected
console output — covering startup/exit and the todo/deadline/event/
list/mark/unmark commands. Add the test-ui skill
(.claude/skills/test-ui/SKILL.md), which compiles the program fresh,
runs each test case's input through it, and diffs the actual output
against the plan character for character, stopping immediately and
reporting actual vs. expected on the first mismatch. Update AGENTS.md
so both the test plan and the skill are kept in the post-code-change
workflow.

Keeping expected output as plain text in a Markdown file (rather than
a script with embedded assertions) keeps the test plan readable and
editable by a student, while letting an AI agent do the mechanical
work of running and diffing that the old shell scripts used to do.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add error handling for invalid and incomplete commands
commitResults.messageBody:
Bott assumes every command is well-formed: an empty "todo", a
"deadline" without "/by", a "mark" with no or an out-of-range task
number, or a command it doesn't recognize at all either throws an
uncaught exception or silently does the wrong thing, instead of
telling the user what went wrong.

Let's add BottException, a checked exception for errors specific to
Bott, per the A-Exceptions extension. executeCommand() now throws it
for each way a command can be invalid, with a message specific to
that failure (e.g. distinguishing a missing "/by" marker from an
empty date/time after it) and a "Try: ..." hint showing the correct
form, rather than one generic error for every case. main()'s loop
catches BottException around each command and prints it as an
"OOPS!!!" message without ending the session.

Giving each failure its own specific, actionable message (the
extension's stretch goal) costs little extra code here since the
parsing was already broken into small per-command helpers, and it
saves the user from guessing what they typed wrong. Add TC7 and TC8
to test/ui-test-plan.md covering the two minimal required errors
(empty todo description, unknown command) plus the deadline/event/
mark-specific ones.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add task deletion; switch task storage to ArrayList
commitResults.messageBody:
Bott has no way to remove a task once added, and tasks are stored in
a fixed-size Task[] sized by an assumed 100-task cap, which the
A-Collections extension asks to replace with a proper collection.

Let's add a "delete <n>" command, handled by a new deleteTask() that
reuses the existing parseTaskNumber() helper so its missing/invalid/
out-of-range error messages stay consistent with mark/unmark. Switch
the task list itself from Task[] plus a manually threaded taskCount
to a List<Task> backed by ArrayList, removing the MAX_TASKS cap and
the taskCount parameter/return value that executeCommand(), addTask(),
buildTaskListMessage(), and setTaskStatus() all had to pass around,
since tasks.size() is now authoritative.

Using a List rather than swapping in a differently-sized array keeps
add/delete O(1)/O(n) with no capacity planning, and simplifies the
method signatures throughout the file as a side effect. Add TC9/TC10
to test/ui-test-plan.md covering delete's normal behavior (including
list renumbering after repeated deletes) and its error cases, and
update TC7 for the new command list in the "unknown command" message.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add TaskType enum for task-type icons
commitResults.messageBody:
Each of Todo, Deadline, and Event independently hardcodes its own
type-letter literal ("[T]"/"[D]"/"[E]") inside its toString()
override; the A-Enums extension asks to use enums where a variable
in the code can naturally be represented as one, and this fixed,
closed set of related constants is exactly that case.

Let's add a TaskType enum (TODO/DEADLINE/EVENT) that owns each
type's icon via getIcon(). Task gains a TaskType field, set through
its constructor, and its toString() now renders both the type icon
and the status icon in one place. Todo's toString() override becomes
unnecessary and is removed; Deadline's and Event's overrides drop
their hardcoded prefix and just append their own suffix to
super.toString().

Centralizing the type-to-icon mapping in the enum removes the
duplicated literals without changing any output — verified against
the full ui-test-plan.md, which still passes byte-for-byte. Command
words (list/mark/todo/...) and the isDone flag were also considered
but left as-is: the command switch is already a clean String switch
per the style guide's own example, and isDone is an idiomatic
boolean per the style guide's boolean-naming convention, so an enum
would add indirection without a matching gain in clarity for either.

commitResults.messageTitle: docs/README.md: Document all commands and error handling
commitResults.messageBody:
The user guide is still the unfilled project template: placeholder
sections ("Feature ABC", "Feature XYZ"), a placeholder title comment,
and only one real section ("Adding deadlines") with generic filler
text instead of Bott's actual behavior.

Let's fill in a Quick Start section and one section per command
(todo, deadline, event, list, mark, unmark, delete, bye), each with
a real command and its expected console output, plus an "Error
handling" section covering the OOPS!!! messages, and a command
summary table at the end.

Every example output was generated by running the compiled program
rather than typed by hand, and verified byte-for-byte against that
output, so the guide can't silently drift from what Bott actually
prints.

commitResults.messageTitle: Save and load tasks from a file
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks only live in memory, so the whole list is lost every time
Bott exits.

Users expect their tasks to still be there the next time they
start the program, so the in-memory list needs to be backed by
persistent storage.

Let's,
* add Task#toFileFormat(), overridden by Deadline and Event, to
  serialize each task to a "|"-delimited line (e.g.
  "D | 0 | return book | June 6th")
* load tasks from data/bott.txt once at startup, skipping and
  logging any corrupted line instead of crashing
* save the full list after every add, delete, mark, and unmark,
  rather than only on exit

Saving after every mutation is simplest to reason about and
avoids losing data if the program is killed instead of exited
normally via "bye".

Since tasks now persist between runs, update ui-test-plan.md and
the test-ui skill so test cases reset data/bott.txt between runs
(keeping them independent), add TC11 to cover save/load across a
restart, and ignore data/bott.txt in .gitignore.

commitResults.messageTitle: Deadline/Event: store dates as LocalDate, not free text
commitResults.messageBody:
Deadline and Event store their dates as plain strings, so users can
type anything ("Sunday", "Aug 6th 2pm") and the same value is echoed
back unchanged.

Free-text dates can't be validated, sorted, or compared, and there's
no consistent way to display them back to the user.

Let's,
* store "by"/"from"/"to" as java.time.LocalDate instead of String
* accept dates from the user in yyyy-MM-dd format (e.g. 2019-10-15)
  and display them as MMM dd yyyy (e.g. Oct 15 2019)
* add Bott#parseDate() so deadline/event parsing rejects an invalid
  or malformed date with a specific error naming the field, the bad
  value, and the expected format, instead of crashing or silently
  storing garbage

LocalDate (rather than LocalDateTime) is enough here since neither
the required input format nor the display format carries a time
component.

Update ui-test-plan.md: TC3, TC4, TC6, TC8, TC9, and TC11 now use
yyyy-MM-dd input and MMM dd yyyy expected output, and a new TC12
exercises invalid-date handling (bad format, a nonexistent calendar
date, and recovery afterward).

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract Ui class; make Bott instance-based
commitResults.messageBody:
Bott is one large class where main() and its static helper methods
directly call System.out/Scanner for every user-facing message
(banner, task acknowledgements, errors, farewell) alongside command
parsing, task storage, and the task list itself.

Mixing all four responsibilities in one class makes it harder to see
which code deals with the user versus the data, and stands in the
way of extracting the other pieces (Storage, Parser, TaskList) called
for by the class-design target.

Let's,
* add Ui, owning all console I/O: the welcome banner, reading a
  command line, the divider-wrapped message printer, and one method
  per kind of acknowledgement/error Bott used to print inline
* convert Bott from a fully-static class to an instance with `ui`
  and `tasks` fields, a constructor that loads saved tasks, an
  instance run() holding the former main() loop, and a main() that
  just does `new Bott().run()`
* have every Bott method that used to print directly call the
  matching Ui method instead

This is the first of several extractions moving Bott toward
Storage/Parser/TaskList/Ui, taking Ui first since it's the most
self-contained of the four (it only needs the Task objects it's
told to print, not the storage or parsing logic).

Parsing methods (parseTodo, parseDeadline, parseEvent, parseDate,
parseTaskNumber) and the save-file methods stay static for now,
since they don't depend on Bott's instance state; they'll move to
Parser and Storage in later iterations.

Verified with the test-ui skill: all 12 documented test cases still
produce byte-identical output.

Bott's save-file logic (loadTasks(), parseSavedTask(), saveTasks(),
and the SAVED_TASKS_FILE_PATH constant) lives directly in Bott,
alongside command parsing and the task list, even though none of it
needs Bott's other state.

Bundling file I/O into the same class as everything else makes Bott
bigger than it needs to be and stands in the way of the remaining
Parser/TaskList extractions the class-design target calls for.

Let's,
* add Storage, constructed with a file path, exposing load() and
  save(List<Task>)
* have Bott's constructor take a filePath parameter and build
  `storage = new Storage(filePath); tasks = storage.load();`,
  matching the target skeleton's constructor shape
* have main() pass SAVED_TASKS_FILE_PATH to `new Bott(...)`

One deliberate change in the process: saveTasks() used to catch its
IOException and call ui.showError(...) directly, which would have
made Storage depend on Ui just to report a write failure. Instead,
Storage.save() now throws BottException, which addTask/deleteTask/
setTaskStatus let propagate to the same top-level catch in run()
that already handles every other command error. The user sees the
identical "OOPS!!! Could not save tasks: ..." message; Storage now
has no knowledge of Ui at all.

The save-file's corrupted-line diagnostic stays a plain
System.out.println inside Storage rather than being routed through
Ui, since threading Ui into Storage for one diagnostic line isn't
worth the coupling; this can be revisited later if wanted.

Verified with the test-ui skill: all 12 documented test cases still
produce byte-identical output. Also manually verified the save-
failure path (by making the save file's path an unwritable
directory) still reports the same "OOPS!!!" message via the
propagated exception.

Bott holds the task list as a raw List<Task> field and manipulates it
directly (tasks.add(...), tasks.remove(taskNumber - 1), etc.) inline
in addTask/deleteTask/setTaskStatus, mixing "how the list is stored"
with command handling.

The class-design target calls for a dedicated TaskList that owns the
list and its operations, which also means Bott no longer needs to
know the list is backed by java.util.List, or repeat the "-1" for
1-based task numbers at every call site.

Let's,
* add TaskList, wrapping a List<Task> with add(task),
  remove(taskNumber), get(taskNumber), and size() - all taking
  1-based positions, matching how the user refers to tasks (e.g.
  "mark 2"), so Bott stops converting between 1-based and 0-based
* change Bott's tasks field from List<Task> to TaskList, and update
  addTask/deleteTask/setTaskStatus/executeCommand accordingly
* have Storage.save() and Ui.showTaskList() keep taking a plain
  List<Task>, via TaskList.getTasks(), since neither needs to know
  about TaskList itself - only Bott, which owns the TaskList, does

Storage and Ui's method signatures didn't change; only Bott's calls
to them did (tasks -> tasks.getTasks()).

Verified with the test-ui skill: all 12 documented test cases still
produce byte-identical output.

executeCommand() split the raw input line into a command word and
arguments inline, and Bott held five more parsing methods
(parseTodo, parseDeadline, parseEvent, parseDate, parseTaskNumber)
that turn command arguments into Task objects, dates, and task
numbers - none of which touch ui, storage, or tasks.

This is the last of the four classes called for by the class-design
target. With Storage, TaskList, and Ui already extracted, the
parsing methods were the only remaining piece of Bott that wasn't
really about running the chatbot - they're pure text-to-value
conversions that happened to still live alongside command dispatch.

Let's,
* add Parser, with getCommandWord()/getArguments() (the input-line
  split that used to open executeCommand) plus the five parsing
  methods, moved over unchanged aside from becoming public static
  methods of Parser instead of private static methods of Bott
* have Bott.executeCommand() call Parser.getCommandWord(input) /
  Parser.getArguments(input), and route parsed arguments through
  Parser.parseTodo/parseDeadline/parseEvent/parseTaskNumber

Dispatch itself (deciding which of Bott's own addTask/deleteTask/
setTaskStatus to call for each command word) stays in Bott, since
that requires the ui/tasks/storage instance state Parser doesn't
have - moving it into Parser would need either passing that state
in or introducing a Command object per command, both bigger than
what a "minimal" extraction calls for here.

With this, Bott now only holds the fields, constructor, run() loop,
and the handful of methods that coordinate ui/tasks/storage; every
other responsibility lives in one of Ui/Storage/TaskList/Parser.
Bott.java is down to 134 lines from roughly 450 before this series
of extractions began.

Verified with the test-ui skill: all 12 documented test cases still
produce byte-identical output.

All eleven classes lived unpackaged directly under src/main/java, in
the default package. That's fine for a small starter project, but it
doesn't scale, and several tools (and conventions the codebase will
need later) expect real packages rather than the default one.

Let's organize the classes under a bott root package, split by
responsibility along the same lines as the recent Ui/Storage/Parser/
TaskList extraction:

* bott              - Bott (entry point) and BottException (used
                       across Bott, Parser, and Storage, so it stays
                       in the root package rather than a single-class
                       exception package)
* bott.task         - Task, TaskType, Todo, Deadline, Event, and
                       TaskList (grouped together since TaskList is
                       tightly coupled to Task, not a separate
                       responsibility)
* bott.parser       - Parser
* bott.storage      - Storage
* bott.ui           - Ui

src/main/java stays the source root (nothing moved outside it, and
src/main/java itself was not turned into a package). Each file moved
with `git mv` to preserve history, gained a `package ...;` line, and
gained imports for the classes it references in other packages.

Also updated:
* .claude/skills/test-ui/SKILL.md - compile step now recurses
  (`find src/main/java -name "*.java" | xargs javac -d bin`) instead
  of a flat `src/main/java/*.java` wildcard, since classes are no
  longer all directly under that directory; the run step now invokes
  the fully-qualified `bott.Bott`
* README.md - the "locate Bott.java" IDE instruction now points at
  `src/main/java/bott/Bott.java`

Verified with the test-ui skill (using the updated compile/run
commands): all 12 documented test cases still produce byte-identical
output.

Brings in Gradle build support from the add-gradle-support branch:
build.gradle, the Gradle wrapper scripts (gradlew, gradlew.bat), and
the wrapper jar/properties.

This branch diverged from an old commit (before Bott.java, the
bott.* package structure, and the current test plan/docs existed) and
only ever touched the five Gradle files, so the merge is a clean,
conflict-free addition - nothing on master's side was changed or
removed.

Unlike the first attempt at this merge, build.gradle's mainClass and
shadow-jar name were already fixed to bott.Bott / bott.jar on the
add-gradle-support branch itself before merging, so no follow-up fix
is needed this time.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests for high-value methods; adopt 50% coverage target
commitResults.messageBody:
The project had one JUnit test class (ParserTest, covering only
parseTaskNumber) and no documented policy on what should get a
JUnit test versus relying on the console-level test/ui-test-plan.md.

Without a stated target, coverage tends to drift toward whatever was
touched most recently rather than toward the methods where a bug
would actually hurt - parsing, formatting, and persistence logic.

Let's,
* finish ParserTest: add tests for getCommandWord, getArguments,
  parseTodo, parseDeadline, and parseEvent (parseDate stays
  untested directly, since it's private and fully exercised through
  parseDeadline/parseEvent's date-format test cases)
* add TaskListTest, targeting the 1-based/0-based index conversion
  in add/remove/get directly, since that's a classic off-by-one risk
* add TaskTest, DeadlineTest, and EventTest, covering the toString/
  toFileFormat formatting logic - including the "MMM dd yyyy" display
  format and its zero-padding, which was previously a source of bugs
  in this codebase
* add StorageTest (using JUnit 5's @TempDir), covering save/load
  round-trips, missing-file handling, corrupted-line skipping, and
  the save-failure error path - persistence is the highest-value
  target here, since a bug means data loss
* document a "top ~50% highest-value methods" coverage target in
  AGENTS.md: prioritize parsing/formatting/persistence/boundary
  logic, deprioritize trivial getters and orchestration/interactive
  I/O code that test/ui-test-plan.md already covers, and require
  JUnit tests to be reviewed and updated after every code change
  (not just when something breaks), as step 3 of the existing
  testing workflow

72 tests total, all passing via `./gradlew test`. Deliberately left
untested: Bott, Ui (orchestration/interactive I/O), BottException
(no logic), TaskType and Todo (no logic beyond what TaskTest already
covers generically) - see AGENTS.md for the reasoning.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add missing header comments on 3 methods
commitResults.messageBody:
An audit of every non-private class and method in src/main/java
found 3 without a header comment: Bott.main(), and the
toFileFormat() overrides on Deadline and Event.

The rest of the codebase (all 11 classes, all 8 constructors, and
31 of 34 other non-private methods) was already documented, so these
3 were inconsistencies rather than a systemic gap - notably, the
Deadline/Event toFileFormat() overrides sat right below their
toString() sibling, which did have a comment.

Let's add a one-line comment to main() explaining what it starts,
and comments to both toFileFormat() overrides showing their actual
output format, since Task's base toFileFormat() javadoc's example
doesn't match what these subclasses produce (each appends its own
date field).

Verified with `./gradlew test`: all 72 tests still pass.

This project just adopted the SE-EDU intermediate Java conventions
(seedu-java-coding-standard skill) as mandatory for all Java code,
so the existing code needs to comply too.

Auditing every file against it found two deviations: import
statements in Parser, Storage, Ui, ParserTest, and StorageTest list
this project's own bott.* packages before java.* imports, and the
switch statements in Bott.executeCommand() and
Storage.parseSavedTask() align case labels with switch instead of
indenting them one level under it.

Let's reorder each file's imports to the required static -> java ->
javax -> third-party -> local order, and indent switch case labels
one level under their switch, matching the standard's examples
exactly.

Verified with ./gradlew test (all 72 JUnit tests) and the test-ui
skill (all 12 UI test cases): both pass unchanged, confirming this
is a pure formatting change.

Java code in this project followed CODE_STYLE.md informally, applied
by memory across sessions rather than from a checkable, loadable
reference specific to this repo.

Codifying the standard as a skill means it gets loaded and checked
consistently, rather than depending on whichever conventions happen
to be recalled in a given session.

Let's add a seedu-java-coding-standard skill distilling the SE-EDU
intermediate Java conventions (naming, layout, statement formatting,
comments) into a self-contained checklist, and require AGENTS.md to
invoke it before writing or reviewing any Java code in this project.

A companion commit brings the existing code into compliance with it.

Commit messages in this project followed COMMIT_STYLE.md informally,
the same way Java code followed CODE_STYLE.md before the previous
commit: applied from memory rather than from a checkable, loadable
reference specific to this repo.

Let's add a seedu-git-standard skill distilling the SE-EDU Git
conventions (commit subject/body format, commit granularity, branch
naming) into a self-contained checklist, and require AGENTS.md to
invoke it before proposing or creating any commit message or new
branch name.

The loose "include enough detail" sentence in AGENTS.md's Git
section is removed since the skill now covers that more precisely.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add find command to search tasks by keyword
commitResults.messageBody:
Bott can list every task or act on one by number, but has no way to
locate a task by what it's about - with more than a few tasks, that
means scanning the whole list by eye.

Let's add find <keyword>, listing every task whose description
contains the keyword (matching case-insensitively), renumbered from
1 in the results so they read as their own list rather than implying
positions in the full one.

Split across the existing layers: Task.matchesKeyword() encapsulates
the match check on its own description rather than exposing a raw
getter; TaskList.find() filters to matches, in list order;
Parser.parseFind() validates a non-blank keyword, matching parseTodo's
style; Ui gained showMatchingTasks(), sharing its numbered-listing
logic with showTaskList() via a new showNumberedTasks() helper rather
than duplicating the loop.

Added 13 JUnit tests across TaskTest/TaskListTest/ParserTest, and
TC13 in ui-test-plan.md (match, case-insensitivity, no-match, missing
keyword, and confirming find doesn't alter the underlying list). TC7
and docs/README.md's command list/summary were updated to include
find. All 13 UI test cases and 85 JUnit tests pass.
